steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction and related work for our paper on loss-free machine unlearning, an extension of Selective Synaptic Dampening that needs no labels. Describe the unlearning problem, existing retraining-based and retraining-free methods, and our method.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Machine unlearning: motivation and problem formulation
2. Existing methods: retraining-based vs. retraining-free
3. Limitation: Fisher-based importance needs ground truth labels
4. Our method: Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem
- increasing regulations around ML -> forgetting private or harmful information essential
- split training dataset \mathcal{D} into forget set \mathcal{D}_{f} and retained data \mathcal{D}_{r}=\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{f}
- forget \mathcal{D}_{f}, preserve performance on \mathcal{D}_{r}

2. Existing methods
- disrupt functional mapping for \mathcal{D}_{f} (e.g. random labels) + train a few epochs over \mathcal{D}_{r} to repair/protect performance
- computationally expensive; full dataset stored permanently
- retraining-free: FisherForgetting, Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) (state-of-the-art)
- estimate parameter importance for forget set; disrupt via noise or dampening without destroying retain performance

3. Limitation
- importance via diagonal of Fisher information matrix (FIM) = square of first-order gradients of loss
- needs ground truth label, not always available

4. LFSSD
- extension of SSD without loss or ground truth labels
- replaces Fisher importance with approximation of sensitivity of model to perturbations of each parameter (= parameter importance)
- effective in continual learning, not yet applied in unlearning
- equally effective as Fisher information, no labelled data
- first retraining-free unlearning method needing only unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
As there are more and more regulations around machine learning, it is essential that a trained model is able to forget private or harmful information. This task is usually formulated by splitting a training dataset \mathcal{D} into a subset of data that has to be forgotten \mathcal{D}_{f}, and the retained data \mathcal{D}_{r}=\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{f}. The goal is to forget \mathcal{D}_{f} from the model while at the same time keeping model performance on \mathcal{D}_{r}. Several methods have been proposed to solve this, which disrupt the functional mapping of the model for samples in \mathcal{D}_{f} (e.g. by learning random labels), and also train for a small number of epochs over \mathcal{D}_{r} to repair or protect performance. This is expensive computationally and the full dataset has to be stored permanently.

- retraining-free: FisherForgetting, Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) -> SSD state-of-the-art
- estimate parameter importance for forget set; disrupt via noise or dampening, keep retain set performance
- importance = diagonal of Fisher information matrix (FIM), square of first-order gradients of loss -> needs ground truth label, not always available
- we propose Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD): extension of SSD, no loss or labels
- approximate sensitivity of model to perturbations of each parameter = parameter importance; shown effective in continual learning, not yet in unlearning
- equally effective as Fisher information, no labelled data
- first retraining-free method needing only unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
As there are more and more regulations around machine learning, it is essential that a trained model is able to forget private or harmful information. This task is usually formulated by splitting a training dataset \mathcal{D} into a subset of data that has to be forgotten \mathcal{D}_{f}, and the retained data \mathcal{D}_{r}=\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{f}. The goal is to forget \mathcal{D}_{f} from the model while at the same time keeping model performance on \mathcal{D}_{r}. Several methods have been proposed to solve this, which disrupt the functional mapping of the model for samples in \mathcal{D}_{f} (e.g. by learning random labels), and also train for a small number of epochs over \mathcal{D}_{r} to repair or protect performance. This is expensive computationally and the full dataset has to be stored permanently.

More recent methods such as FisherForgetting or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) have looked at approaches that need no retraining, and SSD achieves state-of-the-art performance. These methods often estimate how important parameters are for the forget set, so that these parameters can be disrupted through noise or dampening without destroying performance on the retain set. Parameter importance is usually estimated with the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is computed as the square of the first-order gradients of the loss. This needs a ground truth label, and this may not always be available. So we propose a new extension of SSD that does not need access to the loss or to ground truth labels, which we call Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD). LFSSD replaces the importance estimation based on Fisher with an approximation of how sensitive the model is to perturbations of each parameter, which can be interpreted as parameter importance. This kind of importance estimation has been shown to work in continual learning, but it has not been used in unlearning yet. Here we show that this new way of dampening important parameters is as effective as Fisher information, without needing labelled data. As far as we know, LFSSD is the first unlearning method without retraining that only needs the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability of a trained model to forget private or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting a training dataset \mathcal{D} into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten \mathcal{D}_{f}, and the retained data \mathcal{D}_{r}=\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{f}. The objective is to forget \mathcal{D}_{f} from the model while simultaneously preserving model performance on \mathcal{D}_{r} [1]. To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt the model's functional mapping for samples in \mathcal{D}_{f} (e.g. by learning random labels), while also training for a small number of epochs over \mathcal{D}_{r} to repair or protect performance [2,3,4,5,6]. This is computationally expensive and requires permanent storage of the full dataset. In contrast, recent methods such as FisherForgetting from [7] or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from [8] have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set, allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening without destroying performance on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically done via the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be available. We therefore propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss or ground truth labels, which we call Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD). LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance. Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning [9], but has not yet been applied in unlearning. Here, we show that this new approach to dampening important parameters is as effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data. To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

References:
